FIRST read the authoritative build contract at:
SPEC.md

Write EXACTLY THESE THREE files, and nothing else:
1. schedule.js
2. schedule.js
3. schedule.html

The single most important goal: **the instructor updates this page every week by
editing data/schedule.js only, and never touches HTML or CSS.** Design for that.

### data/schedule.js
Assigns `window.SCHEDULE = { weeks: [ ... ] }` as a plain classic script.
Begin with a clear comment block written for a non-programmer explaining: what to
change each week, which fields are required vs optional, the allowed values of
`status`, and a copy-paste template for a new week. Keep formatting regular so
the pattern is obvious by eye.

Each week object:
  { number, dates, topic, summary, readings: [ {label, url} ], due: [ {label, href} ],
    slides: {label, url} | null, status: "past" | "current" | "upcoming",
    kind: "regular" | "exam" | "holiday" | "project" }

Populate all 15 weeks of a real Fall 2026 Python-based intro CS course with a
coherent topic arc: setup & first program, variables/types/IO, conditionals,
loops, functions, strings, lists & dicts, MIDTERM (week 8), file I/O, nested data
& algorithms (search/sort intuition), objects & classes, recursion, testing &
debugging, ethics + a chosen-topic week, final project presentations (week 15).
Give real-looking Fall 2026 week dates (semester starts Mon **Aug 24, 2026**;
include a Thanksgiving break week around Nov 23–27, 2026 — represent that as a
`holiday` entry). Readings should point at free online resources (e.g. Python for
Everybody chapters) — use plausible chapter labels; use `#` for any URL you are
not confident about rather than inventing a broken deep link, and say so in the
comment block. `due` entries link to `assignments.html#<id>` where ids follow the
pattern `ps1`…`ps6`, `lab1`…, `project`.

### assets/schedule.js
Renders the weeks into the page. Requirements:
- Reads `window.SCHEDULE`; if it is missing or has no weeks, render an `.empty`
  message inside the container instead of throwing.
- HTML-escape EVERY interpolated value with `CS101.esc` (including link labels;
  escape `href`/`url` too, and skip rendering a link whose url is falsy).
- Build markup with `.week`, `.week-num`, `.week-dates`, `.week-topic`,
  `.week-readings`, `.week-due`, using `.badge-exam` / `.badge-holiday` /
  `.badge-due` where the spec's vocabulary fits. Mark the `current` week
  distinctly (add an `is-current` class on the `.week` and an accessible
  "This week" label, not colour alone).
- A `.filter-bar` of `.filter-btn` buttons: All / Upcoming / Exams & deadlines.
  Real buttons, `aria-pressed` maintained, filtering purely client-side, and an
  `.empty` state when a filter matches nothing.
- Deep-linking: give each week an id like `week-3` so `schedule.html#week-3`
  scrolls to it, and if the URL has such a hash on load, clear filters so the
  target is actually visible.
- Vanilla JS, no modules, no dependencies beyond the `CS101` helpers.

### schedule.html
Page shell VERBATIM from the spec, `aria-current="page"` on the Schedule nav
link, `<title>Schedule · CS 101</title>`, standard `.page-head`. Inside `<main>`:
a short note telling students the schedule is updated weekly and readings are due
before the Monday lecture, the filter bar container, and the weeks container.
Load `data/schedule.js` then `assets/schedule.js` AFTER `assets/site.js`.
Use ONLY class names from the spec vocabulary. No inline styles.

Add a `<noscript>` note inside `<main>` telling students to see the printable
syllabus if JavaScript is unavailable.

Reply with the list of week topics and confirm the file/date arithmetic is
internally consistent (15 weeks, correct Mondays, break week placed right).

Syllabus

Everything you need to know about how CS 101 runs this semester — what you'll learn, how you'll be graded, and where to get help.

Course description and prerequisites

CS 101 is an introduction to computer science and programming using Python 3. We start from nothing — variables, arithmetic, and printing text — and by December you will be writing programs of several hundred lines that read files, organise data, and solve problems you actually care about. Along the way you'll pick up the habits that separate someone who can write code from someone who can debug it: reading error messages carefully, testing small pieces before assembling big ones, and explaining your reasoning to another person.

This course is designed for students who have never programmed before. That is the default assumption behind every lecture, every lab, and every problem set. If you have programmed before, you are welcome here too, and you'll find the later projects have plenty of room to stretch — but nothing in this course assumes you arrived knowing anything about computers beyond how to open a web browser.

Prerequisites

There is no prerequisite beyond high-school algebra. You should be comfortable with variables in the algebraic sense (x stands for a number), with functions as inputs mapped to outputs, and with basic arithmetic. You do not need calculus, you do not need prior programming, and you do not need to own a powerful computer — see Required materials.

If you're worried you're underprepared, come talk to me in the first two weeks. In my experience that worry is almost always misplaced, and when it isn't, there's usually a small, fixable gap we can close together.

Learning outcomes

By the end of this course you will be able to:

  • Write, run, and debug Python 3 programs of 100–300 lines that read input, transform data, and produce well-formatted output.
  • Decompose a problem statement in plain English into functions with clear inputs, outputs, and responsibilities, and justify that decomposition in writing.
  • Choose appropriately between Python's core data structures — lists, dictionaries, sets, tuples, and strings — and explain the trade-off you made.
  • Trace the execution of a program by hand, predicting the value of every variable at each step, without running it.
  • Read a Python traceback and localise a defect to a specific line, then design a minimal test case that reproduces it.
  • Write functions that read and write text and CSV files, handling missing or malformed data without crashing.
  • Write unit tests for your own functions and explain what each test would catch if it failed.
  • Design, build, document, and present a working program of your own choosing as a final project, and describe its limitations honestly.

Required materials

Textbook

The required textbook is Python for Everybody: Exploring Data Using Python 3 by Charles Severance. It is free — genuinely, permanently free — under a Creative Commons licence, and you can read it online, download the PDF, or buy a printed copy at cost if you prefer paper. You are never required to buy anything for this course. Weekly readings are listed on the Schedule page.

As a second perspective I recommend Runestone Academy's How to Think Like a Computer Scientist: Interactive Edition, which is also free and runs Python directly in the browser. When a concept in one book doesn't click, read the other book's chapter on it before you come to office hours — the two explain things quite differently, and often that's all it takes.

Software

  • Python 3.12 or newer. Free from python.org. We'll install it together in the Week 1 lab, and the lab machines already have it.
  • Visual Studio Code with the official Python extension. Also free. Any editor you already like is fine, but the TAs and I can only promise to debug setup problems in VS Code.
  • A browser-based fallback. If you don't have a laptop that can run VS Code comfortably, you can complete every assignment in this course from a browser using the Runestone interactive textbook and any free browser-based Python environment. Nothing in CS 101 requires software you must install. Tell me in the first week if this is your situation so I can make sure the browser path works smoothly for you.

If you don't have a laptop

The department lends laptops for the full semester, free of charge, no explanation required. This is a normal thing that students do every term and there is no disadvantage to it. Email me or stop by Bishop Hall 214 and I'll start the request the same day.

The Kemper Computer Lab is also open outside class hours with everything already installed.

Assignment and late policy

Problem sets are due Fridays at 11:59 PM and labs are due at the end of your lab section. Submit through the course submission system; a file emailed to me is not a submission unless the system is down, in which case email me and I'll timestamp it manually.

You have six late days for the semester. Spend them however you like, up to three on any single problem set, no explanation and no permission needed — just submit late and I'll apply them automatically. They are for the ordinary chaos of a semester: a bad week, a job shift, a cold, a hard deadline in another class.

After your late days run out

Once you've used all six, late work loses 10% of its earned score per day, up to three days, after which it is no longer accepted and receives a zero. A late day covers any part of a 24-hour period — turning something in at 12:05 AM costs one day, the same as turning it in at 11:00 PM the next night.

Late days do not apply to the midterm, to the final project checkpoint, or to the Week 15 presentation, because those are fixed points that other people's schedules depend on.

When something bigger happens

The late-day budget exists so you never have to explain a normal bad week to me. It is not meant to cover illness, family emergencies, or anything genuinely serious. If that's what's happening, email me — before the deadline if you can, after if you couldn't — and we will work something out. You will not need a doctor's note and I will not ask for details you'd rather not share. I would much rather adjust a deadline than watch a good student fall behind because they were too embarrassed to ask.

Submitting work you're not finished with

Submit it anyway. A partially working program that you've documented honestly — "the file reading works, the sorting doesn't, here's what I think is wrong" — earns substantial partial credit. An empty submission earns none. Writing up what you tried is a real skill and it is graded as one.

Academic integrity

The work you submit must represent your own understanding. That's the whole principle, and everything below is just an application of it to specific situations.

Collaboration

Talking to each other about the course is encouraged and I want you doing it. You may discuss problems, sketch approaches on a whiteboard, explain concepts to each other, and help each other read error messages. What you may not do is share, copy, or transcribe code — yours or anyone else's — including from a screen, a photo, or a repository. A good test: if you can walk away from the conversation, take a break, and then write the solution from your own head, the collaboration was fine. Name your collaborators in a comment at the top of every file. Naming someone is never penalised.

Outside sources

You may read documentation, tutorials, and forum answers. If you adapt more than a line or two from any source, cite it in a comment with a link. Uncited copying from the internet is plagiarism in exactly the way uncited copying from a classmate is.

Generative AI policy

Let me be direct about why this policy is what it is. The exercises in the first two-thirds of this course are not valuable because the resulting programs are valuable — nobody needs another temperature converter. They are valuable because writing them builds something in your head: the ability to hold a program's state in mind, to guess where a bug is before you look, to read a function and know what it does. An AI assistant can produce the artifact instantly and leave that skill entirely unbuilt. Students who lean on one early almost always hit a wall at the midterm, where there is no assistant and the paper doesn't autocomplete.

So the rule is about when and how, not a blanket ban.

Encouraged

  • Asking an AI tool to explain a concept, a piece of syntax, or an error message in different words — the same way you'd ask a tutor.
  • Asking it to generate extra practice problems for you, then solving them yourself.
  • Asking it to review code you have already written and gotten working, and to suggest how you might make it clearer.
  • Using it on the final project for boilerplate outside the core of your idea — plotting setup, argument parsing, file scaffolding — as long as you disclose it and can explain every line.

Not permitted

  • Pasting a lab or problem set prompt into any AI tool, in whole or in part.
  • Submitting code you did not write yourself, whatever produced it.
  • Using AI autocomplete (Copilot and similar) while writing graded work. Turn it off in VS Code before you start; we'll do this together in the Week 1 lab.
  • Using any AI tool during the midterm.

Disclosure

Any use of a generative AI tool that touched your submitted work must be disclosed in a comment at the top of your file: which tool, what you asked it, and what you did with the answer. Two sentences is plenty. Disclosure is not an admission of wrongdoing — permitted use, disclosed, is simply permitted use. Undisclosed use is the violation, even when the use itself would have been allowed.

If something goes wrong

Suspected violations go to the university's academic integrity process, and I follow it consistently because it protects you as much as anyone. But if you're partway into a bad decision — you copied something, you panicked at 3 AM — email me before the deadline. A conversation and a late penalty is a far better outcome for you than a formal report, and I have never once regretted taking that route with a student who came to me first.

Accessibility, accommodations, and support

I want this course to work for you, and I would rather adjust something early than discover in November that it never fit. If any part of how this course is delivered — the pace of lecture, the format of the slides, the lab environment, the exam setting — is a barrier for you, tell me and we'll change it.

Formal accommodations

If you have a documented disability, register with campus Disability Services and have them send me your accommodation letter. You do not have to tell me your diagnosis, and I don't want to know it; the letter is enough. Send it as early in the semester as you can so extended-time exam arrangements are booked before Week 8, but a letter that arrives in Week 10 will still be honoured for everything after it.

Disability Services: contact details on the campus website.

Course materials

Slides, code, and readings are posted before each lecture so you can preview or annotate them. Everything on this site is designed to work with a screen reader and to be readable at large text sizes and on a phone. If you hit something that isn't — a diagram without a description, a colour that's hard to read, a table that won't fit — email me and I'll fix it that week. That's a bug, not an inconvenience.

Well-being and support

Intro programming has a way of feeling personal when it goes badly; a computer telling you that you're wrong forty times in an evening wears on anyone. That feeling is nearly universal in this course and it is not evidence that you don't belong here. If stress, anxiety, money, food, housing, or anything else is making it hard to do this course, campus Counselling and Psychological Services is free and confidential, and I'm glad to help you find the right office if you're not sure where to start. Reaching out early is the version of this that works.

Counselling and Psychological Services: phone and after-hours crisis line on the campus website.

How this course is graded fairly

Every problem set and exam is graded against a written rubric that we publish with the grades, and each question is graded by the same person across all submissions so the standard doesn't drift. Graders don't see your name while grading. If you and a classmate submitted equivalent work, you should get equivalent scores — and if you didn't, I want to know.

Requesting a regrade

Submit regrade requests in writing within 48 hours of grades being released, using the regrade form linked from the assignment page. Say specifically which question you're asking about and which part of the rubric you think was applied incorrectly. "Please look at question 3 again — the rubric gives 2 points for handling an empty file and my code does that on line 41" is a request I can act on in five minutes. "I think I deserve more points" isn't.

I regrade the entire question, so a score can go up, stay the same, or go down — in practice it very rarely goes down. Requests are answered within one week. Asking for a regrade will never count against you, and it doesn't annoy me: a rubric applied wrongly is my mistake, and I'd rather fix it.

Arithmetic errors — points added up wrong, a submitted file missed — aren't regrades. Email me any time and I'll correct them immediately.

Changes to this syllabus

I may adjust the schedule as the semester goes — usually to spend another day on something that's clearly not landing yet. Grading weights, the late-day budget, and the AI policy will not change after Week 2. Any change is announced in lecture and on the forum, and this page is always the current version.

Introduction to Computer Science

This course assumes you have never written a line of code, and it is built that way from the first day to the last. You will learn to read a problem, break it into steps a computer can follow, and write Python 3 that actually runs — slowly, with help, and with plenty of room to get it wrong first.

What you need

A laptop you can bring to lab — any operating system is fine.

Python 3, installed for free from python.org. We will install it together in the first lab if you would rather not do it alone.

The textbook is a free online book; there is nothing to buy for this course. See the syllabus for the link and edition.

This week

Week 3 — Making decisions with conditionals

We are on if, elif and else this week: how a program chooses between two paths, and why the order of your tests matters. Read the textbook sections listed for Week 3 on the schedule before Wednesday's lecture.

Problem Set 2 is due Friday at 11:59 PM. Details, starter files and the grading notes are on the Problem Set 2 page. Start it early enough that you can still come to Thursday's lab with questions.

What you'll learn

Thinking in code

Most of programming is not typing — it is taking something you already know how to do by hand and describing it precisely enough that a machine can repeat it. We spend the first weeks on that translation: variables, conditions, loops, and functions.

Data & structure

Programs are mostly about arranging information so the next step becomes easy. You will learn lists, dictionaries, and files, and — more importantly — how to pick the right one for the problem in front of you.

Building real programs

By the second half of the term you will write programs of a few hundred lines that do something you actually care about. The final project is yours to choose, and we will help you scope it to something finishable.

Debugging & testing

Your code will break constantly. That is not a sign you are bad at this; it is the job. We teach reading error messages, narrowing a bug down with print statements and small tests, and asking for help in a way that gets you a fast answer.

Computing's effect on people

Software decides who gets a loan, what news you see, and whose face a camera recognises. Throughout the term we look at where those systems fail people, so that "it worked on my machine" is never the end of the conversation.

Your first program

This is roughly what week one looks like. Five lines, two ideas: ask the person at the keyboard for something, then use it. Copy it into a file called greet.py, run it, and change the wording — breaking it is the point.

Python 
# greet.py — your first Python 3 program

# input() prints the prompt, waits for you to type, and hands back the text.
name = input("What is your name? ")

# .strip() removes stray spaces; an f-string drops the value into the sentence.
name = name.strip()
print(f"Hello, {name}! Welcome to CS 101.")

How to ask a good question

Include three things and you will usually get an answer in one reply:

  • What you were trying to do, and what you already tried.
  • The exact error message, copied and pasted in full — not paraphrased.
  • The code itself, or the few lines around the problem.

"It doesn't work" is a hard question to answer; "I ran this and got this error" is an easy one.

Expect a reply within one working day. Email sent overnight before a deadline will probably not be answered before that deadline, so please build in a buffer.

If you have accessibility needs, or anything at all going on that affects your coursework, you can raise it privately by email at any point in the term — before, during, or after the fact. You do not need to explain more than you want to.

[Write file: README.md] # CS 101 course website — instructor's guide This folder **is** the website. It is plain HTML, one CSS file, and a little JavaScript: there is no build step, no dependencies, and nothing to install — you edit a file, save it, and that is the new site. If you only read one section, read [The weekly update routine](#the-weekly-update-routine). --- ## File map | File | What it is for | |---|---| | `index.html` | The home page: welcome, "At a glance" facts, the **This week** box you edit weekly, what students will learn, a sample program, and the Contact section. | | `syllabus.html` | The full syllabus: policies, grading, textbook, accommodations. Edited once a term. | | `schedule.html` | The 15-week schedule page. It contains almost no content itself — it draws the weeks from `data/schedule.js`. | | `assignments.html` | The assignments page. Same idea: the list comes from `data/assignments.js`. | | `assets/styles.css` | All the styling for every page — colours, spacing, layout, dark mode. | | `assets/site.js` | Shared behaviour used by every page: the mobile menu button and the "Copy" buttons on code samples. You should not need to touch this. | | `assets/schedule.js` | The code that turns `data/schedule.js` into the visible schedule. Don't edit. | | `assets/assignments.js` | The code that turns `data/assignments.js` into the visible assignment list. Don't edit. | | **`data/schedule.js`** | **Yours to edit.** The 15 weeks: dates, topics, readings, what's due. | | **`data/assignments.js`** | **Yours to edit.** One entry per problem set, exam or project. | | `.nojekyll` | An empty file that tells GitHub Pages to publish the folder exactly as-is. Leave it alone. | | `README.md` | This document. | The rule of thumb: **the two files in `data/` are the ones you edit weekly.** Everything in `assets/` is machinery. --- ## The weekly update routine Fifteen minutes, once a week, usually Monday morning. 1. **Open `data/schedule.js`.** Find the week that is currently marked as the current week and change its `status` to `"done"`. Find the new week and change its `status` to `"current"`. (The file has comments at the top spelling this out; the exact wording of the status values is written there.) 2. **Open `data/assignments.js`** and add the new assignment as one more object in the list — see the worked example below. If an assignment has just closed, you can leave it in place; students like being able to look back at it. 3. **Open `index.html`** and find this comment: ```html ``` Directly under it is the **This week** box. Change the week number, the topic sentence, and the "what's due" sentence. Also fix the two links so they point at the right week and the right assignment: ```html Week 3 on the schedule Problem Set 2 page ``` The `#week-3` and `#ps2` parts must match the `id` values you used in the two data files. If you add `ps4`, the link becomes `assignments.html#ps4`. 4. **Save everything**, then double-click `index.html` to check it looks right (see [Previewing locally](#previewing-locally)). 5. **Commit and push:** ``` git add . git commit -m "Week 4 update" git push ``` Wait a minute or two, then reload the live site. ### Worked example: adding one assignment Open `data/assignments.js`. You will see a list of objects that looks like this. Copy the last one, paste it below, and change the values — keep the commas and the curly braces exactly where they are. ```js window.ASSIGNMENTS = { items: [ // ... earlier assignments above ... { id: "ps3", // used by the link assignments.html#ps3 title: "Problem Set 3: Loops and lists", type: "Problem set", due: "2026-10-02", // always YYYY-MM-DD points: 20, status: "open", summary: "Write three small programs that use for-loops over lists.", details: "Start from ps3_starter.py. Submit a single .py file.", }, ], }; ``` Two things break this file more than anything else: a **missing comma** between two objects, and a **quote you forgot to close**. If the page goes blank, that is almost certainly why — see [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting). --- ## Previewing locally **The quick way:** double-click `index.html`. It opens in your browser and everything works. (Browsers restrict the clipboard on `file://` pages, but the Copy buttons have a built-in fallback, so they still work.) **The exact way** — identical to how it will behave when published: open a terminal in this folder and run ``` python3 -m http.server 8000 ``` then visit in your browser. Press `Ctrl+C` in the terminal to stop it. --- ## Free hosting ### GitHub Pages (recommended) 1. Create a free account at github.com if you don't have one. 2. Create a new, empty repository — for example `cs101-fall-2026`. Public is simplest; Pages works with public repos on the free plan. 3. From this folder, push the site up (GitHub shows you these exact commands when the repo is created): ``` git init git add . git commit -m "Initial course site" git branch -M main git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/cs101-fall-2026.git git push -u origin main ``` 4. In the repository on github.com go to **Settings → Pages**. 5. Under "Build and deployment", set **Source** to *Deploy from a branch*, choose branch **`main`** and folder **`/ (root)`**, and click **Save**. 6. Your site appears at: ``` https://YOUR-USERNAME.github.io/cs101-fall-2026/ ``` Every `git push` after that republishes the site automatically. **Changes take one to two minutes to appear** — if you reload instantly you will see the old page, which is normal. **What `.nojekyll` does:** GitHub Pages would otherwise run your files through a blog engine called Jekyll, which ignores some folders and can mangle files. The empty `.nojekyll` file switches that off so your folder is published byte for byte. Never delete it. ### Equally free alternatives - **Cloudflare Pages** — drag this folder onto the dashboard, or connect the same GitHub repo; free, no card required. - **Netlify** — same story: drag-and-drop the folder at app.netlify.com/drop and it is live in seconds. A **custom domain** (like `cs101.youruniversity.edu`) is optional and works on all three. Registering a domain is the only part of this that ever costs money — the hosting itself is free on every option above. --- ## Common tasks **Change a due date.** Open `data/assignments.js`, find the assignment, change its `due` value. Keep the `YYYY-MM-DD` format. If the date is also mentioned in `data/schedule.js` for that week, change it there too. **Add a week.** Open `data/schedule.js` and copy an existing week object, paste it at the end of the list, and change the week number, dates, topic and readings. Keep the `id` values in the `week-N` pattern so `schedule.html#week-16` keeps working. **Add a code example.** Copy this block into any page inside a `
`, and give the `id` a name no other block on that page uses (here, `snip-loop`). The `data-copy-target` must match the `id` exactly — that is what wires up the Copy button. ```html
Python 
for i in range(3):
    print(i)
``` Write the code with real line breaks and real indentation inside the `` tag; if your example contains `<`, `>` or `&`, write them as `<`, `>` and `&`. **Change the accent colour.** Open `assets/styles.css`, look at the top for the `:root` block, and change the `--accent` value (it is an indigo by default). `--accent-contrast` is the text colour used *on top of* the accent, so if you pick a light accent, set that to a dark colour to keep text readable. **Fix a broken link.** All links in this site are relative and lowercase — for example `href="schedule.html"`, not a full `https://` address. Check that the filename matches exactly, including case, and that anything after a `#` matches an `id` that really exists on the target page. --- ## Troubleshooting **The page went blank after I edited a data file.** This is nearly always a missing comma or an unclosed quote. Open the page in your browser, press **F12**, and click the **Console** tab: you will see a red message like `Uncaught SyntaxError: ... line 42`. Go to that line number in the data file and look at it and the line above it. Check that every entry ends with `},` and that every piece of text has a quote at both ends. If you get stuck, undo your edit (`Ctrl+Z` repeatedly) back to a working state and redo it in smaller steps. **My changes aren't showing up.** If you are viewing the live site, wait one to two minutes for the deploy to finish. Then force the browser to fetch fresh files with a hard refresh: `Ctrl+Shift+R` (Windows/Linux) or `Cmd+Shift+R` (Mac).     Assignment and late policy

    222

    Problem sets are due Fridays at 11:59 PM and labs are due at the end of your lab section. Submit through the course submission system; a file emailed to me is not a submission unless the system is down, in which case email me and I'll timestamp it manually.

    223
    224

    You have six late days for the semester. Spend them however you like, up to three on any single problem set, no explanation and no permission needed — just submit late and I'll apply them automatically. They are for the ordinary chaos of a semester: a bad week, a job shift, a cold, a hard deadline in another class.

    225
    226

    After your late days run out

    227

    Once you've used all six, late work loses 10% of its earned score per day, up to three days, after which it is no longer accepted and receives a zero. A late day covers any part of a 24-hour period — turning something in at 12:05 AM costs one day, the same as turning it in at 11:00 PM the next night.

    228

    Late days do not apply to the midterm, to the final project checkpoint, or to the Week 15 presentation, because those are fixed points that other people's schedules depend on.

    229

    When something bigger happens

    230

    The late-day budget exists so you never have to explain a normal bad week to me. It is not meant to cover illness, family emergencies, or anything genuinely serious. If that's what's happening, email me — before the deadline if you can, after if you couldn't — and we will work something out. You will not need a doctor's note and I will not ask for details you'd rather not share. I would much rather adjust a deadline than watch a good student fall behind because they were too embarrassed to ask.

    231

    Submitting work you're not finished with

    232

    Submit it anyway. A partially working program that you've documented honestly — "the file reading works, the sorting doesn't, here's what I think is wrong" — earns substantial partial credit. An empty submission earns none. Writing up what you tried is a real skill and it is graded as one.

    234

    Academic integrity

    239

    The work you submit must represent your own understanding. That's the whole principle, and everything below is just an application of it to specific situations.

    240

    Collaboration

    241

    Talking to each other about the course is encouraged and I want you doing it. You may discuss problems, sketch approaches on a whiteboard, explain concepts to each other, and help each other read error messages. What you may not do is share, copy, or transcribe code — yours or anyone else's — including from a screen, a photo, or a repository. A good test: if you can walk away from the conversation, take a break, and then write the solution from your own head, the collaboration was fine. Name your collaborators in a comment at the top of every file. Naming someone is never penalised.

    242

    Outside sources

    243

    You may read documentation, tutorials, and forum answers. If you adapt more than a line or two from any source, cite it in a comment with a link. Uncited copying from the internet is plagiarism in exactly the way uncited copying from a classmate is.

    244

    Generative AI policy

    245

    Let me be direct about why this policy is what it is. The exercises in the first two-thirds of this course are not valuable because the resulting programs are valuable — nobody needs another temperature converter. They are valuable because writing them builds something in your head: the ability to hold a program's state in mind, to guess where a bug is before you look, to read a function and know what it does. An AI assistant can produce the artifact instantly and leave that skill entirely unbuilt. Students who lean on one early almost always hit a wall at the midterm, where there is no assistant and the paper doesn't autocomplete.

    246

    So the rule is about when and how, not a blanket ban.

    247

Introduction to Computer Science

Course description and prerequisites

48

CS 101 is an introduction to computer science and programming using Python 3. We start from nothing — variables, arithmetic, and printing text — and by December you will be writing programs of several hundred lines that read files, organise data, and solve problems you actually care about. Along the way you'll pick up the habits that separate someone who can write code from someone who can debug it: reading error messages carefully, testing small pieces before assembling big ones, and explaining your reasoning to another person.

49

This course is designed for students who have never programmed before. That is the default assumption behind every lecture, every lab, and every problem set. If you have programmed before, you are welcome here too, and you'll find the later projects have plenty of room to stretch — but nothing in this course assumes you arrived knowing anything about computers beyond how to open a web browser.

50

Prerequisites

51

There is no prerequisite beyond high-school algebra. You should be comfortable with variables in the algebraic sense (x stands for a number), with functions as inputs mapped to outputs, and with basic arithmetic. You do not need calculus, you do not need prior programming, and you do not need to own a powerful computer — see Required materials.

52

If you're worried you're underprepared, come talk to me in the first two weeks. In my experience that worry is almost always misplaced, and when it isn't, there's usually a small, fixable gap we can close together.

**1. `assets/assignments.js:10` — the `esc` fallback does not escape anything**

```js
var CS101 = window.CS101 || {};
var esc = CS101.esc || function (value) { return String(value == null ? '' : value); };
```

**2. `assets/assignments.js:228` — `decodeURIComponent` can throw and kills the `hashchange` wiring**

```js
var wanted = decodeURIComponent(String(window.location.hash || '').replace(/^#/, ''));
```

A malformed percent-escape in the URL (`assignments.html#%`, `#%zz`, `#50%`) makes `decodeURIComponent` throw `URIError`. `goToHash()` is called synchronously at line 236, *before* `window.addEventListener('hashchange', goToHash)` on line 237 — so the throw propagates out of `init()` and line 237 never runs. The list still renders (that happened earlier), but hash navigation is dead for the rest of the page's life, and the console shows an uncaught error. Minimal fix: wrap the decode in `try { … } catch (e) { wanted = hash.replace(/^#/, ''); }`, or move the `goToHash()` call to after the `addEventListener`.

**3. `assets/assignments.js:32-39` — `formatDate` validates the month but not the day**

```js
if (month < 0 || month > 11) return text;
var date = new Date(Date.UTC(year, month, day));
return DAYS[date.getUTCDay()] + ' ' + day + ' ' + MONTHS[month] + ' ' + year;
```

`day` is never range-checked, and `Date.UTC` rolls over silently. A typo like `"2026-09-31"` produces `Date.UTC(2026, 8, 31)` → 1 Oct (Thursday), and the function prints `"Thu 31 Sep 2026"` — day and month come from the string, weekday from the rolled-over date, so the weekday is wrong and the impossible date is displayed as if valid. `"2026-09-00"` gives `"Mon 0 Sep 2026"`. Minimal fix: after constructing `date`, bail out with `return text;` unless `date.getUTCDate() === day && date.getUTCMonth() === month`.

Course description and prerequisites

48

CS 101 is an introduction to computer science and programming using Python 3. We start from nothing — variables, arithmetic, and printing text — and by December you will be writing programs of several hundred lines that read files, organise data, and solve problems you actually care about. Along the way you'll pick up the habits that separate someone who can write code from someone who can debug it: reading error messages carefully, testing small pieces before assembling big ones, and explaining your reasoning to another person.

49

This course is designed for students who have never programmed before. That is the default assumption behind every lecture, every lab, and every problem set. If you have programmed before, you are welcome here too, and you'll find the later projects have plenty of room to stretch — but nothing in this course assumes you arrived knowing anything about computers beyond how to open a web browser.

50

Prerequisites

51

There is no prerequisite beyond high-school algebra. You should be comfortable with variables in the algebraic sense (x stands for a number), with functions as inputs mapped to outputs, and with basic arithmetic. You do not need calculus, you do not need prior programming, and you do not need to own a powerful computer — see Required materials.

52

If you're worried you're underprepared, come talk to me in the first two weeks. In my experience that worry is almost always misplaced, and when it isn't, there's usually a small, fixable gap we can close together.

Assignment and late policy

222

Problem sets are due Fridays at 11:59 PM and lab projects are due at 11:59 PM on the Thursday after they are handed out. Submit through the course submission system; a file emailed to me is not a submission unless the system is down, in which case email me and I'll timestamp it manually.

Spend them however you like, up to three on any single problem set, no explanation and no permission needed — just submit late and I'll apply them automatically. They are for the ordinary chaos of a semester: a bad week, a job shift, a cold, a hard deadline in another class.

After your late days run out

227

Once you've used all six, late work loses 10% of its earned score per day, up to three days, after which it is no longer accepted and receives a zero. A late day covers any part of a 24-hour period — turning something in at 12:05 AM costs one day, the same as turning it in at 11:00 PM the next night.

Late days do not apply to the midterm, to the final project proposal, or to the Week 15 presentation, because those are fixed points that other people's schedules depend on.

When something bigger happens

230

The late-day budget exists so you never have to explain a normal bad week to me. It is not meant to cover illness, family emergencies, or anything genuinely serious. If that's what's happening, email me — before the deadline if you can, after if you couldn't — and we will work something out. You will not need a doctor's note and I will not ask for details you'd rather not share. I would much rather adjust a deadline than watch a good student fall behind because they were too embarrassed to ask.

231

Submitting work you're not finished with

232

Submit it anyway. A partially working program that you've documented honestly — "the file reading works, the sorting doesn't, here's what I think is wrong" — earns substantial partial credit. An empty submission earns none. Writing up what you tried is a real skill and it is graded as one.

Academic integrity

239

The work you submit must represent your own understanding. That's the whole principle, and everything below is just an application of it to specific situations.

240

Collaboration

241

Talking to each other about the course is encouraged and I want you doing it. You may discuss problems, sketch approaches on a whiteboard, explain concepts to each other, and help each other read error messages. What you may not do is share, copy, or transcribe code — yours or anyone else's — including from a screen, a photo, or a repository. A good test: if you can walk away from the conversation, take a break, and then write the solution from your own head, the collaboration was fine. Name your collaborators in a comment at the top of every file. Naming someone is never penalised.

242

Outside sources

243

You may read documentation, tutorials, and forum answers. If you adapt more than a line or two from any source, cite it in a comment with a link. Uncited copying from the internet is plagiarism in exactly the way uncited copying from a classmate is.

244

Generative AI policy

245

Let me be direct about why this policy is what it is. The exercises in the first two-thirds of this course are not valuable because the resulting programs are valuable — nobody needs another temperature converter. They are valuable because writing them builds something in your head: the ability to hold a program's state in mind, to guess where a bug is before you look, to read a function and know what it does. An AI assistant can produce the artifact instantly and leave that skill entirely unbuilt. Students who lean on one early almost always hit a wall at the midterm, where there is no assistant and the paper doesn't autocomplete.

246

So the rule is about when and how, not a blanket ban.

247

Encouraged

248
    249
  • Asking an AI tool to explain a concept, a piece of syntax, or an error message in different words — the same way you'd ask a tutor.
    • 250
  • Asking it to generate extra practice problems for you, then solving them yourself.
    • 251
  • Asking it to review code you have already written and gotten working, and to suggest how you might make it clearer.
    • 252
  • Using it on the final project for boilerplate outside the core of your idea — plotting setup, argument parsing, file scaffolding — as long as you disclose it and can explain every line.
    • 253

Not permitted

256
    257
  • Pasting a lab or problem set prompt into any AI tool, in whole or in part.
    • 258
  • Submitting code you did not write yourself, whatever produced it.
    • 259
  • Using AI autocomplete (Copilot and similar) while writing graded work. Turn it off in VS Code before you start; we'll do this together in the Week 1 lab.
    • 260
  • Using any AI tool during the midterm.

Disclosure

264

Any use of a generative AI tool that touched your submitted work must be disclosed in a comment at the top of your file: which tool, what you asked it, and what you did with the answer. Two sentences is plenty. Disclosure is not an admission of wrongdoing — permitted use, disclosed, is simply permitted use. Undisclosed use is the violation, even when the use itself would have been allowed.

Suspected violations go to the university's academic integrity process, and I follow it consistently because it protects you as much as anyone. But if you're partway into a bad decision — you copied something, you panicked at 3 AM — email me before the deadline. Parallel work drifted in exactly the places you'd expect, and I fixed all of it:

Neither was "right" — there was no source of truth to be right against. Three agents produced three different lab counts, and I picked one.

| File | Claimed | Backed by real content? |
|---|---|---|
| `syllabus.html` | 13 graded labs | No — a bare number in a grading table |
| `data/schedule.js` | `lab1`–`lab11` | No — invented titles, no assignments behind them |
| `data/assignments.js` | `lab1`–`lab4` | **Yes** — full tasks, starter code, rubrics |

I made the assignments file win, because it was the only one where the labs actually existed. The other two were asserting a count without anything behind it, so conforming them cost nothing; conforming the assignments file would have meant inventing seven more labs from scratch.

## How it happened

My fault, and specifically traceable. I wrote the shared contract before fanning the agents out, and in the id list I wrote:

```
ps1…ps6, lab1…, project
```

I bounded the problem sets and left the labs open-ended. The assignments agent got an explicit `lab1`–`lab4` in its own prompt, so it built four. The schedule agent had only that unbounded `lab1…`, so it did the reasonable thing and extrapolated a lab per teaching week — eleven. Both agents followed their instructions correctly; the instructions disagreed.

The syllabus's 13 is a separate instance of the same gap: I never told that agent the assignment inventory at all, and my own prompt seeded it with the phrase "weekly labs" as an example grading component. It invented a plausible number to fill in.

The common cause is that I pinned the lab count in exactly one of three prompts. A file-ownership table isn't enough for values that appear in multiple files — those need to be stated once, identically, in every prompt that touches them.

## Worth a second look

Four graded labs is now internally consistent, but it is a real pedagogical change from what two of your three pages originally described, and it's your call rather than mine:

- **Thursday lab still meets every week** — attendance and in-class exercises sit under the 10% participation line.
- **Only four labs are graded artifacts**, in Weeks 9–13, worth 15% total. Before the midterm the graded work is the six problem sets.

If you'd rather have a graded lab most weeks — which is a defensible design for intro CS, and closer to what the syllabus originally claimed — that means writing roughly nine more lab assignments with starter code and rubrics. Course description and prerequisites

48

CS 101 is an introduction to computer science and programming using Python 3. We start from nothing — variables, arithmetic, and printing text — and by December you will be writing programs of several hundred lines that read files, organise data, and solve problems you actually care about. Along the way you'll pick up the habits that separate someone who can write code from someone who can debug it: reading error messages carefully, testing small pieces before assembling big ones, and explaining your reasoning to another person.

49

This course is designed for students who have never programmed before. That is the default assumption behind every lecture, every lab, and every problem set. If you have programmed before, you are welcome here too, and you'll find the later projects have plenty of room to stretch — but nothing in this course assumes you arrived knowing anything about computers beyond how to open a web browser.

50

Prerequisites

51

There is no prerequisite beyond high-school algebra. You should be comfortable with variables in the algebraic sense (x stands for a number), with functions as inputs mapped to outputs, and with basic arithmetic. You do not need calculus, you do not need prior programming, and you do not need to own a powerful computer — see Required materials.

52

If you're worried you're underprepared, come talk to me in the first two weeks. In my experience that worry is almost always misplaced, and when it isn't, there's usually a small, fixable gap we can close together.

Learning outcomes

59

By the end of this course you will be able to:

60
    61
  • Write, run, and debug Python 3 programs of 100–300 lines that read input, transform data, and produce well-formatted output.
    • 62
  • Decompose a problem statement in plain English into functions with clear inputs, outputs, and responsibilities, and justify that decomposition in writing.
    • 63
  • Choose appropriately between Python's core data structures — lists, dictionaries, sets, tuples, and strings — and explain the trade-off you made.
    • 64
  • Trace the execution of a program by hand, predicting the value of every variable at each step, without running it.
    • 65
  • Read a Python traceback and localise a defect to a specific line, then design a minimal test case that reproduces it.
    • 66
  • Write functions that read and write text and CSV files, handling missing or malformed data without crashing.
    • 67
  • Write unit tests for your own functions and explain what each test would catch if it failed.
    • 68
  • Design, build, document, and present a working program of your own choosing as a final project, and describe its limitations honestly.

Textbook

You are never required to buy anything for this course. Weekly readings are listed on the Schedule page.

As a second perspective I recommend Runestone Academy's How to Think Like a Computer Scientist: Interactive Edition, which is also free and runs Python directly in the browser. When a concept in one book doesn't click, read the other book's chapter on it before you come to office hours — the two explain things quite differently, and often that's all it takes.

Assignment and late policy

222

Problem sets are due Fridays at 11:59 PM and lab projects are due at 11:59 PM on the Thursday after they are handed out. Submit through the course submission system; a file emailed to me is not a submission unless the system is down, in which case email me and I'll timestamp it manually.

223
224

You have six late days for the semester. Spend them however you like, up to three on any single problem set, no explanation and no permission needed — just submit late and I'll apply them automatically. They are for the ordinary chaos of a semester: a bad week, a job shift, a cold, a hard deadline in another class.

225
226

After your late days run out

227

Once you've used all six, late work loses 10% of its earned score per day, up to three days, after which it is no longer accepted and receives a zero. A late day covers any part of a 24-hour period — turning something in at 12:05 AM costs one day, the same as turning it in at 11:00 PM the next night.

228

Late days do not apply to the midterm, to the final project proposal, or to the Week 15 presentation, because those are fixed points that other people's schedules depend on.

229

When something bigger happens

230

The late-day budget exists so you never have to explain a normal bad week to me. It is not meant to cover illness, family emergencies, or anything genuinely serious. If that's what's happening, email me — before the deadline if you can, after if you couldn't — and we will work something out. You will not need a doctor's note and I will not ask for details you'd rather not share. I would much rather adjust a deadline than watch a good student fall behind because they were too embarrassed to ask.

231

Submitting work you're not finished with

232

Submit it anyway. A partially working program that you've documented honestly — "the file reading works, the sorting doesn't, here's what I think is wrong" — earns substantial partial credit. An empty submission earns none. Writing up what you tried is a real skill and it is graded as one.

Academic integrity

239

The work you submit must represent your own understanding. That's the whole principle, and everything below is just an application of it to specific situations.

240

Collaboration

241

Talking to each other about the course is encouraged and I want you doing it. You may discuss problems, sketch approaches on a whiteboard, explain concepts to each other, and help each other read error messages. What you may not do is share, copy, or transcribe code — yours or anyone else's — including from a screen, a photo, or a repository. A good test: if you can walk away from the conversation, take a break, and then write the solution from your own head, the collaboration was fine. Name your collaborators in a comment at the top of every file. Naming someone is never penalised.

242

Outside sources

243

You may read documentation, tutorials, and forum answers. If you adapt more than a line or two from any source, cite it in a comment with a link. Uncited copying from the internet is plagiarism in exactly the way uncited copying from a classmate is.

244

Generative AI policy

245

Let me be direct about why this policy is what it is. The exercises in the first two-thirds of this course are not valuable because the resulting programs are valuable — nobody needs another temperature converter. They are valuable because writing them builds something in your head: the ability to hold a program's state in mind, to guess where a bug is before you look, to read a function and know what it does. An AI assistant can produce the artifact instantly and leave that skill entirely unbuilt. Students who lean on one early almost always hit a wall at the midterm, where there is no assistant and the paper doesn't autocomplete.

246

So the rule is about when and how, not a blanket ban.

247

Encouraged

248
    249
  • Asking an AI tool to explain a concept, a piece of syntax, or an error message in different words — the same way you'd ask a tutor.
    • 250
  • Asking it to generate extra practice problems for you, then solving them yourself.
    • 251
  • Asking it to review code you have already written and gotten working, and to suggest how you might make it clearer.
    • 252
  • Using it on the final project for boilerplate outside the core of your idea — plotting setup, argument parsing, file scaffolding — as long as you disclose it and can explain every line.
    • 253
254

Not permitted

256
    257
  • Pasting a lab or problem set prompt into any AI tool, in whole or in part.
    • 258
  • Submitting code you did not write yourself, whatever produced it.
    • 259
  • Using AI autocomplete (Copilot and similar) while writing graded work. Turn it off in VS Code before you start; we'll do this together in the Week 1 lab.
    • 260
  • Using any AI tool during the midterm.
    • 261

Disclosure

264

Any use of a generative AI tool that touched your submitted work must be disclosed in a comment at the top of your file: which tool, what you asked it, and what you did with the answer. Two sentences is plenty. Disclosure is not an admission of wrongdoing — permitted use, disclosed, is simply permitted use. Undisclosed use is the violation, even when the use itself would have been allowed.

265

If something goes wrong

266

Suspected violations go to the university's academic integrity process, and I follow it consistently because it protects you as much as anyone. But if you're partway into a bad decision — you copied something, you panicked at 3 AM — email me before the deadline. A conversation and a late penalty is a far better outcome for you than a formal report, and I have never once regretted taking that route with a student who came to me first.

Accessibility, accommodations, and support

274

I want this course to work for you, and I would rather adjust something early than discover in November that it never fit. If any part of how this course is delivered — the pace of lecture, the format of the slides, the lab environment, the exam setting — is a barrier for you, tell me and we'll change it.

275

Formal accommodations

276

If you have a documented disability, register with campus Disability Services and have them send me your accommodation letter. You do not have to tell me your diagnosis, and I don't want to know it; the letter is enough. Send it as early in the semester as you can so extended-time exam arrangements are booked before Week 8, but a letter that arrives in Week 10 will still be honoured for everything after it.

277

Disability Services: contact details on the campus website.

278

Course materials

279

Slides, code, and readings are posted before each lecture so you can preview or annotate them. Everything on this site is designed to work with a screen reader and to be readable at large text sizes and on a phone. If you hit something that isn't — a diagram without a description, a colour that's hard to read, a table that won't fit — email me and I'll fix it that week. That's a bug, not an inconvenience.

280

Well-being and support

281

Intro programming has a way of feeling personal when it goes badly; a computer telling you that you're wrong forty times in an evening wears on anyone. That feeling is nearly universal in this course and it is not evidence that you don't belong here. If stress, anxiety, money, food, housing, or anything else is making it hard to do this course, campus Counselling and Psychological Services is free and confidential, and I'm glad to help you find the right office if you're not sure where to start. Reaching out early is the version of this that works.

Counselling and Psychological Services: phone and after-hours crisis line on the campus website.

How this course is graded fairly

290

Every problem set and exam is graded against a written rubric that we publish with the grades, and each question is graded by the same person across all submissions so the standard doesn't drift. Graders don't see your name while grading. If you and a classmate submitted equivalent work, you should get equivalent scores — and if you didn't, I want to know.

291

Requesting a regrade

292

Submit regrade requests in writing within 48 hours of grades being released, using the regrade form linked from the assignment page. Say specifically which question you're asking about and which part of the rubric you think was applied incorrectly. "Please look at question 3 again — the rubric gives 2 points for handling an empty file and my code does that on line 41" is a request I can act on in five minutes. "I think I deserve more points" isn't.

293

I regrade the entire question, so a score can go up, stay the same, or go down — in practice it very rarely goes down. Requests are answered within one week. Asking for a regrade will never count against you, and it doesn't annoy me: a rubric applied wrongly is my mistake, and I'd rather fix it.

294

Arithmetic errors — points added up wrong, a submitted file missed — aren't regrades. Email me any time and I'll correct them immediately.

Course description and prerequisites

48

CS 101 is an introduction to computer science and programming using Python 3. We start from nothing — variables, arithmetic, and printing text — and by December you will be writing programs of several hundred lines that read files, organise data, and solve problems you actually care about. Along the way you'll pick up the habits that separate someone who can write code from someone who can debug it: reading error messages carefully, testing small pieces before assembling big ones, and explaining your reasoning to another person.

49

This course is designed for students who have never programmed before. That is the default assumption behind every lecture, every lab, and every problem set. If you have programmed before, you are welcome here too, and you'll find the later projects have plenty of room to stretch — but nothing in this course assumes you arrived knowing anything about computers beyond how to open a web browser.

50

Prerequisites

51

There is no prerequisite beyond high-school algebra. You should be comfortable with variables in the algebraic sense (x stands for a number), with functions as inputs mapped to outputs, and with basic arithmetic. You do not need calculus, you do not need prior programming, and you do not need to own a powerful computer — see Required materials.

52

If you're worried you're underprepared, come talk to me in the first two weeks. In my experience that worry is almost always misplaced, and when it isn't, there's usually a small, fixable gap we can close together.

Assignment and late policy

222

Problem sets are due Fridays at 11:59 PM and labs are due at 11:59 PM on the Thursday after they are handed out. Two labs get a longer window because there is no lab section in between: the Week 7 lab is due after midterm week, and the Week 13 lab is due after Thanksgiving break. The Schedule page lists every lab's actual due week. Submit through the course submission system; a file emailed to me is not a submission unless the system is down, in which case email me and I'll timestamp it manually.

223
224

You have six late days for the semester. Spend them however you like, up to three on any single problem set, no explanation and no permission needed — just submit late and I'll apply them automatically. They are for the ordinary chaos of a semester: a bad week, a job shift, a cold, a hard deadline in another class.

After your late days run out

227

Once you've used all six, late work loses 10% of its earned score per day, up to three days, after which it is no longer accepted and receives a zero. A late day covers any part of a 24-hour period — turning something in at 12:05 AM costs one day, the same as turning it in at 11:00 PM the next night.

228

Late days do not apply to the midterm, to the final project proposal, or to the Week 15 presentation, because those are fixed points that other people's schedules depend on.

229

When something bigger happens

230

The late-day budget exists so you never have to explain a normal bad week to me. It is not meant to cover illness, family emergencies, or anything genuinely serious. If that's what's happening, email me — before the deadline if you can, after if you couldn't — and we will work something out. You will not need a doctor's note and I will not ask for details you'd rather not share. I would much rather adjust a deadline than watch a good student fall behind because they were too embarrassed to ask.

231

Submitting work you're not finished with

232

Submit it anyway. A partially working program that you've documented honestly — "the file reading works, the sorting doesn't, here's what I think is wrong" — earns substantial partial credit. An empty submission earns none. Writing up what you tried is a real skill and it is graded as one.

Academic integrity

239

The work you submit must represent your own understanding. That's the whole principle, and everything below is just an application of it to specific situations.

240

Collaboration

241

Talking to each other about the course is encouraged and I want you doing it. You may discuss problems, sketch approaches on a whiteboard, explain concepts to each other, and help each other read error messages. What you may not do is share, copy, or transcribe code — yours or anyone else's — including from a screen, a photo, or a repository. A good test: if you can walk away from the conversation, take a break, and then write the solution from your own head, the collaboration was fine. Name your collaborators in a comment at the top of every file. Naming someone is never penalised.

242

Outside sources

243

You may read documentation, tutorials, and forum answers. If you adapt more than a line or two from any source, cite it in a comment with a link. Uncited copying from the internet is plagiarism in exactly the way uncited copying from a classmate is.

244

Generative AI policy

245

Let me be direct about why this policy is what it is. The exercises in the first two-thirds of this course are not valuable because the resulting programs are valuable — nobody needs another temperature converter. They are valuable because writing them builds something in your head: the ability to hold a program's state in mind, to guess where a bug is before you look, to read a function and know what it does. An AI assistant can produce the artifact instantly and leave that skill entirely unbuilt. Students who lean on one early almost always hit a wall at the midterm, where there is no assistant and the paper doesn't autocomplete.

246

So the rule is about when and how, not a blanket ban.

Encouraged

248
    249
  • Asking an AI tool to explain a concept, a piece of syntax, or an error message in different words — the same way you'd ask a tutor.
    • 250

    • 252

    • 258

  • Using AI autocomplete (Copilot and similar) while writing graded work. Turn it off in VS Code before you start; we'll do this together in the Week 1 lab.

Any use of a generative AI tool that touched your submitted work must be disclosed in a comment at the top of your file: which tool, what you asked it, and what you did with the answer. Two sentences is plenty. Disclosure is not an admission of wrongdoing — permitted use, disclosed, is simply permitted use. Undisclosed use is the violation, even when the use itself would have been allowed.

If something goes wrong

266

Suspected violations go to the university's academic integrity process, and I follow it consistently because it protects you as much as anyone. But if you're partway into a bad decision — you copied something, you panicked at 3 AM — email me before the deadline. A conversation and a late penalty is a far better outcome for you than a formal report, and I have never once regretted taking that route with a student who came to me first.

I want this course to work for you, and I would rather adjust something early than discover in November that it never fit. If any part of how this course is delivered — the pace of lecture, the format of the slides, the lab environment, the exam setting — is a barrier for you, tell me and we'll change it.

276

If you have a documented disability, register with campus Disability Services and have them send me your accommodation letter. You do not have to tell me your diagnosis, and I don't want to know it; the letter is enough. Send it as early in the semester as you can so extended-time exam arrangements are booked before Week 8, but a letter that arrives in Week 10 will still be honoured for everything after it.

Everything on this site is designed to work with a screen reader and to be readable at large text sizes and on a phone. If you hit something that isn't — a diagram without a description, a colour that's hard to read, a table that won't fit — email me and I'll fix it that week. That's a bug, not an inconvenience.

Well-being and support

281

Intro programming has a way of feeling personal when it goes badly; a computer telling you that you're wrong forty times in an evening wears on anyone. That feeling is nearly universal in this course and it is not evidence that you don't belong here. If stress, anxiety, money, food, housing, or anything else is making it hard to do this course, campus Counselling and Psychological Services is free and confidential, and I'm glad to help you find the right office if you're not sure where to start. Reaching out early is the version of this that works.

Every problem set and exam is graded against a written rubric that we publish with the grades, and each question is graded by the same person across all submissions so the standard doesn't drift. Submit regrade requests in writing within 48 hours of grades being released, using the regrade form linked from the assignment page. Say specifically which question you're asking about and which part of the rubric you think was applied incorrectly. "Please look at question 3 again — the rubric gives 2 points for handling an empty file and my code does that on line 41" is a request I can act on in five minutes. I regrade the entire question, so a score can go up, stay the same, or go down — in practice it very rarely goes down. Requests are answered within one week. Asking for a regrade will never count against you, and it doesn't annoy me: a rubric applied wrongly is my mistake, and I'd rather fix it.

Thinking in code

120

Most of programming is not typing — it is taking something you already know how to do 121 by hand and describing it precisely enough that a machine can repeat it. We spend the 122 first weeks on that translation: variables, conditions, loops, and functions.

Course description and prerequisites

48

CS 101 is an introduction to computer science and programming using Python 3. We start from nothing — variables, arithmetic, and printing text — and by December you will be writing programs of several hundred lines that read files, organise data, and solve problems you actually care about. Along the way you'll pick up the habits that separate someone who can write code from someone who can debug it: reading error messages carefully, testing small pieces before assembling big ones, and explaining your reasoning to another person.

49

This course is designed for students who have never programmed before. That is the default assumption behind every lecture, every lab, and every problem set. If you have programmed before, you are welcome here too, and you'll find the later projects have plenty of room to stretch — but nothing in this course assumes you arrived knowing anything about computers beyond how to open a web browser.

50

Prerequisites

51

There is no prerequisite beyond high-school algebra. You should be comfortable with variables in the algebraic sense (x stands for a number), with functions as inputs mapped to outputs, and with basic arithmetic. You do not need calculus, you do not need prior programming, and you do not need to own a powerful computer — see Required materials.

52

If you're worried you're underprepared, come talk to me in the first two weeks. In my experience that worry is almost always misplaced, and when it isn't, there's usually a small, fixable gap we can close together.

Assignment and late policy

222

Problem sets are due Fridays at 11:59 PM and labs are due at 11:59 PM on the Thursday after they are handed out. Two labs get a longer window because there is no lab section in between: the Week 7 lab is due after midterm week, and the Week 13 lab is due after Thanksgiving break. The Schedule page lists every lab's actual due week. Submit through the course submission system; a file emailed to me is not a submission unless the system is down, in which case email me and I'll timestamp it manually.

223
224

You have six late days for the semester. Spend them however you like, up to three on any single problem set, no explanation and no permission needed — just submit late and I'll apply them automatically. They are for the ordinary chaos of a semester: a bad week, a job shift, a cold, a hard deadline in another class.

225
226

After your late days run out

227

Once you've used all six, late work loses 10% of its earned score per day, up to three days, after which it is no longer accepted and receives a zero. A late day covers any part of a 24-hour period — turning something in at 12:05 AM costs one day, the same as turning it in at 11:00 PM the next night.

228

Late days do not apply to the midterm, to the final project proposal, or to the Week 15 presentation, because those are fixed points that other people's schedules depend on.

229

When something bigger happens

230

The late-day budget exists so you never have to explain a normal bad week to me. It is not meant to cover illness, family emergencies, or anything genuinely serious. If that's what's happening, email me — before the deadline if you can, after if you couldn't — and we will work something out. You will not need a doctor's note and I will not ask for details you'd rather not share. I would much rather adjust a deadline than watch a good student fall behind because they were too embarrassed to ask.

231

Submitting work you're not finished with

232

Submit it anyway. A partially working program that you've documented honestly — "the file reading works, the sorting doesn't, here's what I think is wrong" — earns substantial partial credit. An empty submission earns none. Writing up what you tried is a real skill and it is graded as one.

Academic integrity

239

The work you submit must represent your own understanding. That's the whole principle, and everything below is just an application of it to specific situations.

240

Collaboration

241

Talking to each other about the course is encouraged and I want you doing it. You may discuss problems, sketch approaches on a whiteboard, explain concepts to each other, and help each other read error messages. What you may not do is share, copy, or transcribe code — yours or anyone else's — including from a screen, a photo, or a repository. A good test: if you can walk away from the conversation, take a break, and then write the solution from your own head, the collaboration was fine. Name your collaborators in a comment at the top of every file. Naming someone is never penalised.

242

Outside sources

243

You may read documentation, tutorials, and forum answers. If you adapt more than a line or two from any source, cite it in a comment with a link. Uncited copying from the internet is plagiarism in exactly the way uncited copying from a classmate is.

244

Generative AI policy

245

Let me be direct about why this policy is what it is. The exercises in the first two-thirds of this course are not valuable because the resulting programs are valuable — nobody needs another temperature converter. They are valuable because writing them builds something in your head: the ability to hold a program's state in mind, to guess where a bug is before you look, to read a function and know what it does. An AI assistant can produce the artifact instantly and leave that skill entirely unbuilt. Students who lean on one early almost always hit a wall at the midterm, where there is no assistant and the paper doesn't autocomplete.

246

So the rule is about when and how, not a blanket ban.

247

Encouraged

248
    249
  • Asking an AI tool to explain a concept, a piece of syntax, or an error message in different words — the same way you'd ask a tutor.
    • 250
  • Asking it to generate extra practice problems for you, then solving them yourself.
    • 251
  • Asking it to review code you have already written and gotten working, and to suggest how you might make it clearer.
    • 252
  • Using it on the final project for boilerplate outside the core of your idea — plotting setup, argument parsing, file scaffolding — as long as you disclose it and can explain every line.

256
    257
  • Pasting a lab or problem set prompt into any AI tool, in whole or in part.
    • 258
  • Submitting code you did not write yourself, whatever produced it.
    • 259
  • Using AI autocomplete (Copilot and similar) while writing graded work. Turn it off in VS Code before you start; we'll do this together in the Week 1 lab.
    • 260
  • Using any AI tool during the midterm.

Disclosure

264

Any use of a generative AI tool that touched your submitted work must be disclosed in a comment at the top of your file: which tool, what you asked it, and what you did with the answer. Two sentences is plenty. Disclosure is not an admission of wrongdoing — permitted use, disclosed, is simply permitted use. Undisclosed use is the violation, even when the use itself would have been allowed.

If something goes wrong

266

Suspected violations go to the university's academic integrity process, and I follow it consistently because it protects you as much as anyone. But if you're partway into a bad decision — you copied something, you panicked at 3 AM — email me before the deadline. A conversation and a late penalty is a far better outcome for you than a formal report, and I have never once regretted taking that route with a student who came to me first.

274

I want this course to work for you, and I would rather adjust something early than discover in November that it never fit. If any part of how this course is delivered — the pace of lecture, the format of the slides, the lab environment, the exam setting — is a barrier for you, tell me and we'll change it.

276

If you have a documented disability, register with campus Disability Services and have them send me your accommodation letter. You do not have to tell me your diagnosis, and I don't want to know it; the letter is enough. Send it as early in the semester as you can so extended-time exam arrangements are booked before Week 8, but a letter that arrives in Week 10 will still be honoured for everything after it.

Slides, code, and readings are posted before each lecture so you can preview or annotate them. Everything on this site is designed to work with a screen reader and to be readable at large text sizes and on a phone. If you hit something that isn't — a diagram without a description, a colour that's hard to read, a table that won't fit — email me and I'll fix it that week. That's a bug, not an inconvenience.

Well-being and support

281

Intro programming has a way of feeling personal when it goes badly; a computer telling you that you're wrong forty times in an evening wears on anyone. That feeling is nearly universal in this course and it is not evidence that you don't belong here. If stress, anxiety, money, food, housing, or anything else is making it hard to do this course, campus Counselling and Psychological Services is free and confidential, and I'm glad to help you find the right office if you're not sure where to start. Reaching out early is the version of this that works.

Every problem set and exam is graded against a written rubric that we publish with the grades, and each question is graded by the same person across all submissions so the standard doesn't drift. Graders don't see your name while grading. If you and a classmate submitted equivalent work, you should get equivalent scores — and if you didn't, I want to know.

Requesting a regrade

Submit regrade requests in writing within 48 hours of grades being released, using the regrade form linked from the assignment page. Say specifically which question you're asking about and which part of the rubric you think was applied incorrectly. "Please look at question 3 again — the rubric gives 2 points for handling an empty file and my code does that on line 41" is a request I can act on in five minutes. "I think I deserve more points" isn't.

I regrade the entire question, so a score can go up, stay the same, or go down — in practice it very rarely goes down. Requests are answered within one week. Asking for a regrade will never count against you, and it doesn't annoy me: a rubric applied wrongly is my mistake, and I'd rather fix it.
