Course description and prerequisites

48

CS 101 is an introduction to computer science and programming using Python 3. We start from nothing — variables, arithmetic, and printing text — and by December you will be writing programs of several hundred lines that read files, organise data, and solve problems you actually care about. Along the way you'll pick up the habits that separate someone who can write code from someone who can debug it: reading error messages carefully, testing small pieces before assembling big ones, and explaining your reasoning to another person.

49

This course is designed for students who have never programmed before. That is the default assumption behind every lecture, every lab, and every problem set. If you have programmed before, you are welcome here too, and you'll find the later projects have plenty of room to stretch — but nothing in this course assumes you arrived knowing anything about computers beyond how to open a web browser.

50

Prerequisites

51

There is no prerequisite beyond high-school algebra. You should be comfortable with variables in the algebraic sense (x stands for a number), with functions as inputs mapped to outputs, and with basic arithmetic. You do not need calculus, you do not need prior programming, and you do not need to own a powerful computer — see Required materials.

52

If you're worried you're underprepared, come talk to me in the first two weeks. In my experience that worry is almost always misplaced, and when it isn't, there's usually a small, fixable gap we can close together.

Assignment and late policy

222

Problem sets are due Fridays at 11:59 PM and labs are due at 11:59 PM on the Thursday after they are handed out. Two labs get a longer window because there is no lab section in between: the Week 7 lab is due after midterm week, and the Week 13 lab is due after Thanksgiving break. The Schedule page lists every lab's actual due week. Submit through the course submission system; a file emailed to me is not a submission unless the system is down, in which case email me and I'll timestamp it manually.

223
224

You have six late days for the semester. Spend them however you like, up to three on any single problem set, no explanation and no permission needed — just submit late and I'll apply them automatically. They are for the ordinary chaos of a semester: a bad week, a job shift, a cold, a hard deadline in another class.

225
226

After your late days run out

227

Once you've used all six, late work loses 10% of its earned score per day, up to three days, after which it is no longer accepted and receives a zero. A late day covers any part of a 24-hour period — turning something in at 12:05 AM costs one day, the same as turning it in at 11:00 PM the next night.

228

Late days do not apply to the midterm, to the final project proposal, or to the Week 15 presentation, because those are fixed points that other people's schedules depend on.

229

When something bigger happens

230

The late-day budget exists so you never have to explain a normal bad week to me. It is not meant to cover illness, family emergencies, or anything genuinely serious. If that's what's happening, email me — before the deadline if you can, after if you couldn't — and we will work something out. You will not need a doctor's note and I will not ask for details you'd rather not share. I would much rather adjust a deadline than watch a good student fall behind because they were too embarrassed to ask.

231

Submitting work you're not finished with

232

Submit it anyway. A partially working program that you've documented honestly — "the file reading works, the sorting doesn't, here's what I think is wrong" — earns substantial partial credit. An empty submission earns none. Writing up what you tried is a real skill and it is graded as one.

Academic integrity

239

The work you submit must represent your own understanding. That's the whole principle, and everything below is just an application of it to specific situations.

240

Collaboration

241

Talking to each other about the course is encouraged and I want you doing it. You may discuss problems, sketch approaches on a whiteboard, explain concepts to each other, and help each other read error messages. What you may not do is share, copy, or transcribe code — yours or anyone else's — including from a screen, a photo, or a repository. A good test: if you can walk away from the conversation, take a break, and then write the solution from your own head, the collaboration was fine. Name your collaborators in a comment at the top of every file. Naming someone is never penalised. The one exception to writing it from your own head is the weekly labs, which you may complete with one partner — put both names in the file header and each of you submits — while problem sets and the midterm remain strictly individual work.

242

Outside sources

243

You may read documentation, tutorials, and forum answers. If you adapt more than a line or two from any source, cite it in a comment with a link. Uncited copying from the internet is plagiarism in exactly the way uncited copying from a classmate is.

244

Generative AI policy

245

Let me be direct about why this policy is what it is. The exercises in the first two-thirds of this course are not valuable because the resulting programs are valuable — nobody needs another temperature converter. They are valuable because writing them builds something in your head: the ability to hold a program's state in mind, to guess where a bug is before you look, to read a function and know what it does. An AI assistant can produce the artifact instantly and leave that skill entirely unbuilt. Students who lean on one early almost always hit a wall at the midterm, where there is no assistant and the paper doesn't autocomplete.

246

So the rule is about when and how, not a blanket ban.

247

Encouraged

248
    249
  • Asking an AI tool to explain a concept, a piece of syntax, or an error message in different words — the same way you'd ask a tutor.
    • 250
  • Asking it to generate extra practice problems for you, then solving them yourself.
    • 251
  • Asking it to review code you have already written and gotten working, and to suggest how you might make it clearer.
    • 252
  • Using it on the final project for boilerplate outside the core of your idea — plotting setup, argument parsing, file scaffolding — as long as you disclose it and can explain every line.

  • Pasting a lab or problem set prompt into any AI tool, in whole or in part.
    • 258
  • Submitting code you did not write yourself, whatever produced it.
    • 259
  • Using AI autocomplete (Copilot and similar) while writing graded work. Turn it off in VS Code before you start; we'll do this together in the Week 1 lab.

Disclosure

264

Any use of a generative AI tool that touched your submitted work must be disclosed in a comment at the top of your file: which tool, what you asked it, and what you did with the answer. Two sentences is plenty. Disclosure is not an admission of wrongdoing — permitted use, disclosed, is simply permitted use. Undisclosed use is the violation, even when the use itself would have been allowed.

265

If something goes wrong

266

Suspected violations go to the university's academic integrity process, and I follow it consistently because it protects you as much as anyone. But if you're partway into a bad decision — you copied something, you panicked at 3 AM — email me before the deadline. A conversation and a late penalty is a far better outcome for you than a formal report, and I have never once regretted taking that route with a student who came to me first.

274

I want this course to work for you, and I would rather adjust something early than discover in November that it never fit. If any part of how this course is delivered — the pace of lecture, the format of the slides, the lab environment, the exam setting — is a barrier for you, tell me and we'll change it.

276

If you have a documented disability, register with campus Disability Services and have them send me your accommodation letter. You do not have to tell me your diagnosis, and I don't want to know it; the letter is enough. Send it as early in the semester as you can so extended-time exam arrangements are booked before Week 8, but a letter that arrives in Week 10 will still be honoured for everything after it.

Disability Services: contact details on the campus website.

Course materials

279

Slides, code, and readings are posted before each lecture so you can preview or annotate them. Everything on this site is designed to work with a screen reader and to be readable at large text sizes and on a phone. If you hit something that isn't — a diagram without a description, a colour that's hard to read, a table that won't fit — email me and I'll fix it that week. That's a bug, not an inconvenience.

280

Well-being and support

281

Intro programming has a way of feeling personal when it goes badly; a computer telling you that you're wrong forty times in an evening wears on anyone. That feeling is nearly universal in this course and it is not evidence that you don't belong here. If stress, anxiety, money, food, housing, or anything else is making it hard to do this course, campus Counselling and Psychological Services is free and confidential, and I'm glad to help you find the right office if you're not sure where to start. Reaching out early is the version of this that works.

Every problem set and exam is graded against a written rubric that we publish with the grades, and each question is graded by the same person across all submissions so the standard doesn't drift. Graders don't see your name while grading. If you and a classmate submitted equivalent work, you should get equivalent scores — and if you didn't, I want to know.

Requesting a regrade

Submit regrade requests in writing within 48 hours of grades being released, using the regrade form linked from the assignment page. "Please look at question 3 again — the rubric gives 2 points for handling an empty file and my code does that on line 41" is a request I can act on in five minutes. "I think I deserve more points" isn't.

I regrade the entire question, so a score can go up, stay the same, or go down — in practice it very rarely goes down. Requests are answered within one week. Asking for a regrade will never count against you, and it doesn't annoy me: a rubric applied wrongly is my mistake, and I'd rather fix it.

## What changed

**`data/assignments.js`** went from 11 assignments to 20 — six problem sets, **13 labs**, and the project (1,865 → 3,658 lines). Labs are **20 points each**, sized for the 2-hour Thursday session, handed out in lab and due the following Thursday:

|---|---|---|
| lab1–lab6 | 1–6 | toolchain, variables, conditionals, loops, functions, strings |

| lab8–lab12 | 9–13 | files, nested data & search/sort, classes, recursion, unittest debugging |
| lab12 | 13 | **two-week window, spans Thanksgiving** |
| lab13 | 14 | ethics case study + chosen topic |

No lab in Week 8, the break week, or Week 15 — which is exactly why the count is 13.

Each lab has a starter file and a worked example **on a different problem** than the graded task. The four old labs weren't discarded: the club roster, grade report, library and recursion material was moved into its correct topic slot and rescaled from 40–45 points down to 20. The old lab4 split in two — recursion became lab11, and the unittest half became lab12, expanded into a bug hunt with three planted bugs.

**Downstream:** the schedule now lists every lab twice (handed out / due) in the correct weeks; the syllabus grading row reads *"Weekly labs (13) — 15%, two lowest dropped"*; the late policy names both long windows; the assignments page lede, the README, and the home page were corrected.

Two independent audits plus a final integrity pass, on top of each writer's own check:

- **All 20 rubrics sum exactly** to their point value — verified item by item, twice.
- **All 42 Python blocks** read line by line: syntax, name resolution, `unittest` guards, recursion base cases, and hand-traced expected output. Zero defects.
- Structure, all 22 cross-file anchors (both directions), lab dates against the calendar, weights summing to 100%, unique filenames, unique DOM ids.

Six real problems surfaced and were fixed: three stale cross-references left by the migration (*"four labs"*, *"Lab 4"*, *"Lab 3"*), an inconsistent partner rule (7 labs allowed pairs, 6 were silent — now uniform and stated in the syllabus), and two absolute integrity clauses that the new pair-work carve-out contradicted — *"may not share, copy, or transcribe code"* and *"submitting code you did not write yourself, whatever produced it"* — both of which would have made lab pairs a policy violation on paper.
